q: Does the paper's pessimistic QAOA-vs-classical crossover (or the Willsch benchmarking trend) hold under newer QAOA variants such as WS-QAOA (warm-start), RQAOA (recursive), and ADAPT-QAOA at the same instance sizes (8-var 2-SAT, 16-var MaxCut, and larger structured instances up to ~24 qubits)?
basis: The replicated paper (Willsch 2020) uses only vanilla QAOA with layered Nelder-Mead. Newer QAOA variants published 2020-2024 (Egger et al. WS-QAOA, Bravyi RQAOA, Zhu ADAPT-QAOA) report substantial improvements in approximation ratio at fixed depth p, and could plausibly shift both the success probability curves in Figs. 7 and 10-11 and any hypothetical runtime crossover point.
next_steps: Extend work/qaoa_core.py with three ansatz variants: (i) WS-QAOA that biases the initial state by a GW rounding, (ii) RQAOA that recursively fixes the largest-|correlation| edge, and (iii) ADAPT-QAOA that greedily adds operators from a mixer pool. Re-run the C3/C4 sweeps at p=1..10 and report success%, r, and total function evaluations vs vanilla QAOA. Free-endpoint budget: pure classical simulation on CherryRd, ~2-4h wall-clock.

q: How do modern classical baselines (Goemans-Williamson SDP with Burer-Monteiro low-rank solvers, branch-and-cut MILP via SCIP, and Tabu/BLS heuristics) compare against QAOA in solution quality and wall-clock time for the exact same 16-var MaxCut instance and scaled-up random weighted MaxCut up to N=100?
basis: The Willsch paper compares QAOA to D-Wave and IBM Q, not to state-of-the-art classical MaxCut solvers. The Guerreschi & Matsuura runtime-crossover claim (~ several hundred qubits) that motivated this slot's brief depends critically on the classical baseline chosen; using a strong heuristic (BLS, KHLWG) rather than plain GW can move the crossover by orders of magnitude.
next_steps: Add work/classical_baselines.py: wrap cvxpy + MOSEK for GW rounding (or SCS if MOSEK unavailable), pyscipopt for exact MILP with 60s timeout, and a numpy Tabu-search implementation. Compare on the C4 16-var instance and on 20 random N in {20,40,60,80,100} G(n,0.5) weighted MaxCut instances. Emit ratio-vs-optimum and time-to-target-ratio curves. Free-endpoint budget: fully local.

q: Does the paper's picture change qualitatively when the graph structure is not Erdos-Renyi-like but instead reflects a real optimization application, e.g. weighted planar (VLSI), power-law (social network community detection), or structured bipartite (portfolio constraints)?
basis: Willsch et al. picked 16-var weighted MaxCut and 2-SAT-8/12/18 to have a unique ground state and highly degenerate first excited states, which is a worst-case-ish scenario for QAOA. Real application graphs often have exploitable structure (locality, community) that both classical heuristics and structured-mixer QAOA can exploit differently.
next_steps: Build a small benchmark set with three graph families: (a) rectangular grid MaxCut N=16..25 via networkx, (b) LFR benchmark graphs at mixing parameter 0.1..0.5, (c) random-regular d=3,4 up to N=24. Run QAOA p=1..5 with the same optimizer stack, plus the classical baselines above. Report whether the p=1 monotone-improvement trend and the linear-anneal-init recovery still hold. Free-endpoint budget: local, ~6h wall-clock.

q: How sensitive is the linear-annealing-init large-p success (Willsch Fig. 10-11; our C5) to realistic noise models: incoherent single-qubit depolarizing, two-qubit correlated ZZ crosstalk, and slow calibration drift across the ~2p*N gate layers?
basis: Our C5 gap (MaxCut p=10 success 76.4% vs paper 85.6%) is currently ascribed to optimizer locality on an ideal simulator; but on real hardware the p=50 2-SAT and p=10 MaxCut runs would traverse thousands of two-qubit gates, and even modest per-gate error rates (~1e-3) compound to depth-limiting infidelity. A noise-model sweep would separate the two effects.
next_steps: Add work/noise_channels.py implementing Kraus operators for single-qubit depolarizing (rates 1e-4..1e-2) and two-qubit ZZ crosstalk. Re-run the C5 linear-init sweeps under three noise budgets. Also add a calibration-drift model: perturb gate angles by Gaussian noise sigma in {0.01, 0.05, 0.1} rad. Report success% vs noise budget for both instances. Free-endpoint budget: density-matrix sim caps at ~14 qubits, so 2-SAT-8A only for full DM; use MC trajectories for 16-var MaxCut.

q: Do hardware advances 2020-2026 (surface-code error-corrected logical qubits, transmon T1/T2 up to milliseconds, native ZZ gates, 100+ high-fidelity qubits on IBM Heron and Quantinuum H2) materially shift the QAOA runtime-vs-classical crossover point implicit in the paper's benchmarking, or is the crossover still gated by algorithmic factors (barren plateaus, optimization overhead)?
basis: The Willsch paper is a 2019/2020 snapshot; QPU capabilities have since improved by ~10x in qubit count and ~2-5x in two-qubit fidelity. The Guerreschi crossover paper is even older (2018). A modern re-analysis would combine the paper's runtime accounting with post-2024 gate times and error rates, and with any published runtime estimates for QAOA on IBM Heron or Quantinuum H2.
next_steps: Literature review: pull cost-model papers (Beverland et al. 2022 resource estimation, IBM Heron whitepaper, Quantinuum H2 benchmarking) and re-derive the QAOA-vs-GW runtime crossover curve under 2026 hardware parameters. Contrast with the Willsch/Guerreschi 2019-2020 assumption stack. Emit a short arXiv-style note. Free-endpoint budget: pure literature and analytic; no sims required.
